Cites JHB

By: Johann Botha | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What is the most trafficked animal in the world - it is the only mammal covered in scales

Unique Selling Point:
The CITES conference of parties is being hosted in South Africa for the first time from Sept 24.

Summary:
When people talk about Cites, it is almost always about elephants and rhinos. And this year is no exception. The big debate is about whether there should be a blanket ban on the sale of ivory and whether all elephants should be moved to Appendix 1, the category offering most protection from illegal trafficking. In the process other "less charismatic" animals and plants don't get much media attention, and therefore also not the protection they need. In our story we look at a few of these: the pangolin, thresher sharks, a fresh water ray from the amazon and a little cardinal fish fighting for survival in northern indonesia. We also look at what has become the biggest threat to many of these animals - the internet! E-bay, whatsapp and even the "dark web" have made it almost impossible to control illegal trade in fauna and flora across international borders. Although technology from silicone valley is also appearing to help conservation officials become more efficient in their jobs.

Press Release:


Cites Tackling Trafficking

The most trafficked animal in the world is the pangolin. Close on its heels are thresher sharks, a freshwater ray endemic to the Amazon Basin and many other species whose survival is threatened. With syndicates plying their lucrative trade in cyber space, cracking down on the scourge has become increasingly complex. Now, the world’s best minds have gathered in
Johannesburg to thrash out trafficking and other crises affecting the planet’s species. Carte Blanche reports on the 17th global CITES conference.


Script:


Cites : All things bright and beautiful...


"Link Derek
on convention centre verandah" "We are at the end of week1 of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on the International Trade in Endangered Species, or, as those in the know call it, Cop17 of Cites
Cites was started back in 1972, when the world realised that we were losing species "
"Vultures
Elephants
Gorillas
Lion
Ivory stockpile
Pangolin being slaughtered" "35000 species listed under Cites
1050 listed on Appendix1
33600 listed on Appendix2" Of the 35 000 species now listed on Cites, about 3% are on appendix 1, banning trade in them altogether, The other listed 96 % can only be traded internationally with special permission
Adam standing at flags in opening plenary Adam Cruise is an international wildlife journalist who follows Citse closely
"Adam talks on camera the overlay
Sequence of cruel shots about animals being killed for the trade mixed with pretty shots" It's got very little to do with the actual animals themselves. Remember this is a trade convention. This is not an animal convention. The title says it – this is a convention in the trade of endangered species. So this is about horse trading amongst countries. Range countries saying ok we can give you so much if you can give us this amount of money. This is what this convention is about, its got nothing to do with conservation. Its got to do with politics, it's got to do with bureaucracy and most importantly, its got to do with money.



W/s of John " John Scanlon, the secretary general for Cites says the planet is in bad shape
"
John Cites General Secretary What we're realising is that we are over exploiting, we can transport things fast to any part of the world and the ability to harvest from nature, there are no limits to that. So Cites is being turned to increasingly.
Shots of convention "Cites: 183 member Countries

2016 COP17
2500 delegates
62 proposals
500 species affected" Every three years all 183 countries who are party to this convention gather somewhere on the planet, adding new species to the list, removing others, and debating and formulating the rules for future trade. This years event is hosted by South Africa, in Sandton and is the biggest meeting of wildlife role players in the planet's history . More than 2500 delegates have begun considering 62 proposals affecting close to 500 species.
"Link Derek
walking down exhibiton aisle" The illegal trade in wild animals and plants is worth around 200 billion US dollars per year, and with that amount at stake the big budgets are aimed at making the most noise, possibly drowning out the causes of species that may not be as charismatic or marketable but are just as threatened.
"Elephants
Cardinal fish " As usual, the big debate is around elephants, but that will only be concluded this coming week. Amidst all the lobbying for this cause, it is easy to forget about species whose plight may be even more dire. Like the Banggai cardinal fish, from northern Indonesia - considered the holy grail by many live fish collectors
"Adam Cruise

Fish being caught" It has a geographic description of just 23 square kilometers. There are about 1.5million of these fish left in this small archepelago, also 500 000 getting pulled out a year. So the maths is simple, 3 years and they're gone.
"Fish thrown into boat

W/s Derek and Alejandro" "Global population decline (since 1995)
90%" While scientist, Alejandro Vagelli studied the little cardinal he realised that unbeknownst to anyone, 90% of their population had already been wiped out, and naively, with his own money and time he tried to stop the trade at Cites in 2007. The proposal was unsuccessful
Alejandro And that was my first attempt to protect this species. If that fish would no be protected, who else would protect it? Boom! No ways.

"Adam


Underwater shot of cardinalfish" He couldn't do it at the next Cop or two because he didn't have any more money, until a Swiss NGO, conservation NGO found him and gave him a little bit of money and he could get it presented to this COP. And really, this is the last throw of the dice for this fish
Freshwater ray swimming in aquarium "Current population status:
Unknown " Another species which may disappear soon in the wild because of aquariums paying good money is this little stingray. What makes the Mobular special from other rays is that it lives in fresh water. It only occurs in the Amazon Basin.
Alejandra From Columbia for example, from 1995 to 2012 more than 500 000 specimens were exported.
Freshwater ray swimming Because it lives in murky water in remote jungles, collecting information was almost impossible, and Bolivias request for listing was rejected in 2013 for lack of data. But Bolivia re-submitted their prposal this year
Alejandra So this time Bolivia felt like they needed, because for them it is important, that they need to present it for Appendix 2, because they have identified issues with the international trade of the species. Because they're just coming and taking this species illegally from their country to basically trade it with other consumers around the world.
"Variety of shark fin market shots
Zambesi sharks swimming
Manta Ray swimming
Dried gill plates
Thresher shark swimming" "100 million sharks killed every year for commercial purposes
Global population decline (past 15 years) 77-99%" The massive demand for shark fins in the far East is decimating our ocean's apex predators. In 2013, Cites listed 5 targeted species of shark and both manta ray species which are killed for their gill plates. This year they're asking for thresher sharks, with its characteristic long tail fin to be added to the list.
"Director, Pew
Oceanic white tip shark swimming
Two hammerhead sharks swimmings
" Already what we've seen is sharks have moved up on the priority list. Although in the past Cites was just focused on the large land animals, now we actually see sharks a key part of the convention's work. A lot of the discussions here and the outreach down in the media centre are really focused on sharks.
Devil Rays swimming "Global population decline (past 15 years)
50 - 99%" They also want the manta rays' smaller relative, the devil ray to be listed, and they're using technology to strengthen the call.
Derek at 3d viewing and then commenting to camera What an awesome experience, virtually swimming with devil rays. Now you can say that this is just clever marketing, but this is what it takes to get some of the lesser known species actually noticed at Cites
"Devil rays swimming
Tania looking at ivory online" Unfortunately, the traffickers are also increasingly using technology and a new proposal on cyber crime was adopted this week
Tania We did an investigation, and in just 6 weeks over 16 countries, we found 30 000 live animals and their body parts available for sale on the internet
"Ground pangolin
Pangolin scales
Pangolin in cage
Baby pangolin
Black bellied pangolin climbing tree" "Pangolins trafficked per year: 100 000 to 200 000

" Which brings us to the only scaled mammal on the planet, the pangolin. And, it is these very scales, which are used for anything from guitar plectrums to traditional Eastern medicine, which has made it the most trafficked animal on the planet. As with the little cardinal fish, this Cop may be their last hope..
"Darryl

Groud pangolin" We really cant afford to lose a single animal. They're so critically endangered I mean as a species at the moment. We might not even have another Cop to feed these proposals because many species might be extinct before the next COP already.
"Various pangolins


Conference rooms
Thresher shark swimming" Good news is that proposals to protect all 8 pangolin species, including our own ground pangolin were accepted this week. Bad news is that no decision is final yet – technically, any proposal can be raised again and overturned by vote in the closing plenery set for this coming wednesday. And, while the whole world is waiting to see if all elephants will be voted onto appendix1, people like Adam caution against expecting the impossible from Cites
"Thresher shark continue
Adam" If it was a conference to preserve the world, what would happen is everything would be listed on Appendix 1. In other words you start with no trade and then you look at the species and say “ooh, ok. This one is doing ok so maybe we can downlist it. In actual fact Cites is the wrong way rround, it's upside down – what they're saying is all species can be traded until proven otherwise.

Promo 10 sec The world’s top conservationists descend on Sandton to answer one question: How can we save pangolin, sharks, elephants and more from extinction?

Promo 15sec "Take a good look at this CardinalFish. You may never see one again.

Upsound

How will top conservationists, gathered in Sandton for Cites Cop 17, save this fish and other animals on the brink of extinction?"



Promo 15sec "Adam: Cites is the wrong way around, it's upside down – what they're saying is all species can be traded until proven otherwise.

To trade not to trade? Global wildlife experts converge on Johannesburg for the 17th CITES conference. Can they save the world’s most fragile species from extinction? "


Of course something has to be done about the massive decimation of elephant populations, and next week we will take a closer look at this, but if you consider that there are still half a million of these elephants left, and that their red data status is only vulnerable, then it seems strange that they should get more attention than this little fish, which, if it isn't protected this year might not be around in three years time

"Link Derek walking down exhibiton aisle" The illegal trade in wild animals and plants is worth around 200 billion US dollars per year, and with that amount at stake the big budgets are aimed at making the most noise, possibly drowning out the causes of species that may not be as charismatic or marketable but are just as threatened. "Elephants Cardinal fish " As usual, the big debate is around elephants, but that will only be concluded this coming week. Amidst all the lobbying for this cause, it is easy to forget about species whose plight may be even more dire. Like the Banggai cardinal fish, from northern Indonesia - considered the holy grail by many live fish collectors "Adam Cruise Fish being caught" It has a geographic description of just 23 square kilometers. There are about 1.5million of these fish left in this small archepelago, also 500 000 getting pulled out a year. So the maths is simple, 3 years and they're gone. "Fish thrown into boat W/s Derek and Alejandro" "Global population decline (since 1995) 90%" While scientist, Alejandro Vagelli studied the little cardinal he realised that unbeknownst to anyone, 90% of their population had already been wiped out, and naively, with his own money and time he tried to stop the trade at Cites in 2007. The proposal was unsuccessful Alejandro And that was my first attempt to protect this species. If that fish would no be protected, who else would protect it? Boom! No ways. "Adam Underwater shot of cardinalfish" He couldn't do it at the next Cop or two because he didn't have any more money, until a Swiss NGO, conservation NGO found him and gave him a little bit of money and he could get it presented to this COP. And really, this is the last throw of the dice for this fish Freshwater ray swimming in aquarium "Current population status: Unknown " Another species which may disappear soon in the wild because of aquariums paying good money is this little stingray. What makes the Mobular special from other rays is that it lives in fresh water. It only occurs in the Amazon Basin. Alejandra From Columbia for example, from 1995 to 2012 more than 500 000 specimens were exported. Freshwater ray swimming Because it lives in murky water in remote jungles, collecting information was almost impossible, and Bolivias request for listing was rejected in 2013 for lack of data. But Bolivia re-submitted their prposal this year Alejandra So this time Bolivia felt like they needed, because for them it is important, that they need to present it for Appendix 2, because they have identified issues with the international trade of the species. Because they're just coming and taking this species illegally from their country to basically trade it with other consumers around the world. "Variety of shark fin market shots Zambesi sharks swimming Manta Ray swimming Dried gill plates Thresher shark swimming" "100 million sharks killed every year for commercial purposes Global population decline (past 15 years) 77-99%" The massive demand for shark fins in the far East is decimating our ocean's apex predators. In 2013, Cites listed 5 targeted species of shark and both manta ray species which are killed for their gill plates. This year they're asking for thresher sharks, with its characteristic long tail fin to be added to the list. "Director, Pew Oceanic white tip shark swimming Two hammerhead sharks swimmings " Already what we've seen is sharks have moved up on the priority list. Although in the past Cites was just focused on the large land animals, now we actually see sharks a key part of the convention's work. A lot of the discussions here and the outreach down in the media centre are really focused on sharks. Devil Rays swimming "Global population decline (past 15 years) 50 - 99%" They also want the manta rays' smaller relative, the devil ray to be listed, and they're using technology to strengthen the call. Derek at 3d viewing and then commenting to camera What an awesome experience, virtually swimming with devil rays. Now you can say that this is just clever marketing, but this is what it takes to get some of the lesser known species actually noticed at Cites "Devil rays swimming Tania looking at ivory online" Unfortunately, the traffickers are also increasingly using technology and a new proposal on cyber crime was adopted this week Tania We did an investigation, and in just 6 weeks over 16 countries, we found 30 000 live animals and their body parts available for sale on the internet "Ground pangolin Pangolin scales Pangolin in cage Baby pangolin Black bellied pangolin climbing tree" "Pangolins trafficked per year: 100 000 to 200 000 " Which brings us to the only scaled mammal on the planet, the pangolin. And, it is these very scales, which are used for anything from guitar plectrums to traditional Eastern medicine, which has made it the most trafficked animal on the planet. As with the little cardinal fish, this Cop may be their last hope.. "Darryl Groud pangolin" We really cant afford to lose a single animal. They're so critically endangered I mean as a species at the moment. We might not even have another Cop to feed these proposals because many species might be extinct before the next COP already. "Various pangolins Conference rooms Thresher shark swimming" Good news is that proposals to protect all 8 pangolin species, including our own ground pangolin were accepted this week. Bad news is that no decision is final yet – technically, any proposal can be raised again and overturned by vote in the closing plenery set for this coming wednesday. And, while the whole world is waiting to see if all elephants will be voted onto appendix1, people like Adam caution against expecting the impossible from Cites "Thresher shark continue Adam" If it was a conference to preserve the world, what would happen is everything would be listed on Appendix 1. In other words you start with no trade and then you look at the species and say “ooh, ok. This one is doing ok so maybe we can downlist it. In actual fact Cites is the wrong way rround, it's upside down – what they're saying is all species can be traded until proven otherwise. Promo 15sec "Take a good look at this CardinalFish. You may never see one again. Upsound How will top conservationists, gathered in Sandton for Cites Cop 17, save this fish and other animals on the brink of extinction?" Promo 15sec "Adam: Cites is the wrong way around, it's upside down – what they're saying is all species can be traded until proven otherwise. To trade not to trade? Global wildlife experts converge on Johannesburg for the 17th CITES conference. Can they save the world’s most fragile species from extinction? " Of course something has to be done about the massive decimation of elephant populations, and next week we will take a closer look at this, but if you consider that there are still half a million of these elephants left, and that their red data status is only vulnerable, then it seems strange that they should get more attention than this little fish, which, if it isn't protected this year might not be around in three years time

metadata.Summary: When people talk about Cites, it is almost always about elephants and rhinos. And this year is no exception. The big debate is about whether there should be a blanket ban on the sale of ivory and whether all elephants should be moved to Appendix 1, the category offering most protection from illegal trafficking. In the process other "less charismatic" animals and plants don't get much media attention, and therefore also not the protection they need. In our story we look at a few of these: the pangolin, thresher sharks, a fresh water ray from the amazon and a little cardinal fish fighting for survival in northern indonesia. We also look at what has become the biggest threat to many of these animals - the internet! E-bay, whatsapp and even the "dark web" have made it almost impossible to control illegal trade in fauna and flora across international borders. Although technology from silicone valley is also appearing to help conservation officials become more efficient in their jobs.
